questions.q: Under a network partition, what choice does the CAP theorem force on a distributed system?
options: Choose between durability of writes and speed of reads
Either refuse some requests (consistency) or serve possibly stale data (availability)
Choose between encryption strength and replication factor
Either drop the partitioned nodes or restart the whole cluster
questions.explanation: When nodes cannot talk, a node either answers from possibly outdated local state or refuses until it can confirm the latest value. CAP says you cannot have both at once.

questions.q: In CAP, what does the C (consistency) actually mean?
options: The database enforces every declared integrity constraint, as the C in ACID does
Replicas eventually converge to a single agreed value
Each transaction moves the data between valid states
Every read reflects the most recent completed write (linearizability)
questions.explanation: CAP's C is linearizability: the system behaves as if there were one copy, and reads never go backwards in time. It is unrelated to ACID's constraint-based C and stronger than eventual convergence.

questions.q: Why can't a distributed system simply 'choose CA' and ignore partitions?
options: Real networks will partition, so tolerance to partitions is not optional
CA is reserved for systems with more than three replicas
Availability mathematically implies partition tolerance, so the choice collapses
Consistency can only be sacrificed after a quorum vote
questions.explanation: Cables break, switches fail, and links time out, so P is a fact of the environment rather than a design option. The real decision is only what to do when a partition happens.

questions.q: During a partition, a CP system that cannot reach quorum typically does what?
options: Continues serving reads and writes from whichever side currently has more clients
Switches to last-write-wins conflict resolution automatically
Refuses or delays requests on the minority side rather than risk stale data
Keeps both sides writable and merges the histories afterward
questions.explanation: A minority cannot know whether the majority has newer writes, so the safe move is to return errors or block until connectivity returns. Correctness is preserved by sacrificing availability there.

questions.q: During a partition, an AP system keeps responding. What is the accepted trade?
options: Writes get throttled down to one per client until the network fully heals
Only read-only requests are honored during the partition window
The minority side shuts down to protect data integrity
Responses may be stale or conflicting and need reconciliation later
questions.explanation: Both sides keep accepting operations from local state, so their histories diverge and must be merged after healing via version vectors, CRDTs, or application logic.

questions.q: Which everyday product behavior smells like an AP design decision?
options: An ATM refusing all withdrawals whenever its bank network link goes down
A shopping cart accepting items offline and merging duplicates later
A ticket site blocking checkout during a datacenter failover
A bank rejecting transfers when a region is unreachable
questions.explanation: The cart favors always accepting the operation and reconciles divergent versions afterward, because a duplicated cart line is cheap to fix. The other three refuse service to protect correctness, which is CP behavior.

questions.q: What does the CAP 'availability' property formally require?
options: Every request to a non-failed node eventually gets a non-error response
The system remains reachable through at least one healthy load balancer at all times
99.99% of requests succeed measured over a month
Failed nodes restart automatically within a bounded time
questions.explanation: CAP availability is an absolute per-request property proven over all executions, not a percentage. Any node still running must answer, which is why a partitioned minority breaks it.

questions.q: Why is 'this database is CP, that one is AP' an oversimplification?
options: CAP labels formally apply only to networks and never to the database software running on them
Vendors alternate between CP and AP with each major release
Many systems are tunable per operation, choosing consistency or availability per request
CP and AP differ only in marketing, not in behavior
questions.explanation: Stores like Cassandra and DynamoDB let each query pick a consistency level, so the same cluster behaves CP for one call and AP for the next. The label describes a default, not a fixed identity.

questions.q: A quorum system has 5 replicas with W=3, R=3. A partition isolates 2 nodes. What happens on the minority side?
options: Writes and quorum reads fail there, since 2 nodes cannot reach quorum
The two nodes elect their own leader and continue operating with W=1 automatically
It serves quorum reads but rejects only the writes
It buffers writes durably and reports them as committed
questions.explanation: Both W and R need three acknowledgements and only two nodes are reachable, so every quorum operation fails. That refusal is exactly what stops the two sides from diverging.

questions.q: What does the PACELC formulation add beyond CAP?
options: A proof that partitions cannot occur in well-built datacenter networks
Even without partitions, systems still trade latency against consistency
A fourth property, elasticity, describing autoscaling behavior
A ranking of consensus protocols by message complexity
questions.explanation: PACELC covers the normal case CAP ignores: else, the choice is latency versus consistency, since strong reads require coordination round trips even on a healthy network.

questions.q: An inventory service shows one item left; two buyers in partitioned regions both purchase it. Which stance did the system take?
options: CP: the system accepted both orders and then canceled one during nightly reconciliation
CA: it prevented the partition by rerouting traffic
AP: it stayed available and now must resolve the oversell after healing
CP: quorum writes allowed both sides to commit safely
questions.explanation: Both sides accepted a write without confirming the global count, which is the availability choice. A CP design would have rejected the minority-side purchase instead of overselling.

questions.q: A coordination service (like ZooKeeper) picks CP. What is the practical consequence during partitions?
options: Reads continue on both sides while writes silently degrade to best-effort delivery semantics
Both sides keep full service using cached membership data
Locks auto-release on both sides so no client ever blocks
The minority partition cannot elect a leader or serve strongly consistent operations
questions.explanation: Leader election and lock grants need a majority, so the minority side stops serving rather than hand out a second lock. That is precisely why such services are trusted for fencing.

questions.q: Why is a single-node relational database not a meaningful example of 'CA'?
options: With one node there is no partition to tolerate, so CAP's trade-off never applies
A single node can never be truly consistent once many concurrent writers become involved
Single nodes are always CP because disks can fail
CA requires at least two datacenters by definition
questions.explanation: CAP describes behavior of a replicated system under partition; with no replicas there is nothing to partition, so calling it CA is vacuous rather than an achievement.

questions.q: Under PACELC, why might a system choose EL (latency over consistency) with no partition present?
options: Regulators require sub-second responses for consumer applications
Consistency checks consume disk and memory capacity that low-latency systems cannot spare
Waiting on cross-replica coordination for every request adds latency users notice
Latency and consistency are equivalent, so the choice is stylistic
questions.explanation: Strong reads need a quorum or leader round trip, which can add tens of milliseconds across regions. Serving from the nearest replica is far faster when slightly stale data is acceptable.

questions.q: DynamoDB offers both eventually consistent and strongly consistent reads. What does choosing strong reads cost you?
options: Strong reads bypass every caching layer, so each one hits cold storage directly instead
Higher read charge and latency, plus unavailability if the leader partition is unreachable
They require a table scan to verify the latest value
Writes must pause while any strong read is in flight
questions.explanation: A strong read must be served by the partition leader, costing double the read units, more latency, and an error when that leader is unreachable. Eventually consistent reads can use any replica.

questions.q: Why does a 2-of-3 quorum system remain available when one node is partitioned away?
options: The missing node's data gets reconstructed instantly from parity blocks on the survivors
Quorum systems always remain available regardless of failures
The partitioned node keeps serving its own clients independently
The majority side still reaches quorum, so operations proceed consistently there
questions.explanation: Two surviving nodes satisfy the majority requirement, so reads and writes overlap on a current copy and continue safely. Only the isolated node loses the ability to serve.

questions.q: A 'CP' database advertises 99.999% availability. How do you reconcile this with CAP?
options: The vendor is lying, since CP systems cannot exceed 99.9% availability
Five nines refers only to reads, which CAP does not constrain
CAP availability is a theoretical guarantee under partitions; five nines is an empirical uptime claim
The system silently switches to AP mode whenever uptime drops
questions.explanation: CAP forbids answering every request during a partition, but partitions are rare and brief, so measured uptime can still be extremely high. The two use the word availability differently.

questions.q: Spanner-style systems claim both strong consistency and very high availability. What makes this practically achievable?
options: Engineering the network (redundant links, majority quorums) makes partitions rare, not impossible
TrueTime physically prevents network partitions from forming
They relax consistency invisibly during business hours
They run every replica inside a single rack to avoid partitions
questions.explanation: Spanner is still CP and would reject minority-side requests, but private redundant fiber and Paxos majorities make those events so rare that observed availability stays near five nines.

questions.q: During partition healing in an AP store, siblings (conflicting versions) surface. Which resolution strategy risks silent data loss?
options: Application-level merge functions that thoughtfully combine fields from both versions
CRDTs designed so concurrent updates merge deterministically
Presenting both versions to the user for a manual choice
Timestamp-based last-write-wins across nodes with unsynchronized clocks
questions.explanation: LWW discards the losing version outright, and with clock skew the discarded one may actually be newer. The other strategies preserve information from both siblings.

questions.q: A payments flow needs linearizable balance checks; feed rendering tolerates staleness. Both hit one datastore. Sound per-CAP design?
options: Choose an AP store everywhere, compensating payment anomalies with client retries
Use per-request consistency levels: quorum reads for payments, relaxed reads for feeds
Serialize all traffic through one leader so both workloads become linearizable
Run two identical strongly consistent clusters and split traffic between them
questions.explanation: Consistency is a per-operation requirement, so paying coordination cost only on balance checks gives correctness where it matters and fast local reads for the feed.
